title: Avoiding the problem won't solve it.
author: Jenny R. Allen
summary: Jenny R. Allen uses a confrontation she dreaded to argue for a specific sequencing rule in hard workplace conversations: get to the problem before you get to the person. The case is a missed data deadline that blew up an executive report and travelled down the chain until it landed on her, even though the colleague responsible did not report to her. Rather than rehearsing an accusation, she applied repeated why questions until the real stake surfaced, which was leadership making decisions without information it needed. Reframing the opening line around that shared stake, with we rather than you, changed what the conversation could produce. It surfaced a data warehouse bug he had been fighting alone, and his own recognition that he should have escalated sooner. Allen is careful about scope: the technique is for restoring a system or a process, and she rules it out for bullying, harassment and ethical lapses, which she classes as boundary violations rather than process failures.
points: The anticipation of a confrontation, not the confrontation itself, is identified as the larger cost, including years of rehearsed retorts.
Repeated why questions convert a personnel grievance into a statement of what the organization actually stands to lose.
Opening with a shared stake rather than an accusation kept the colleague from defending what had not happened and surfaced a technical failure nobody knew about.
The colleague identified his own lapse, failing to escalate, without being told, and the pair left with contingency plans and named owners.
Allen bounds the method explicitly, excluding harm to people and ethical breaches from problem-first framing.
quotes: And not one you can sustain in the workplace. Problems don't disappear just because you avoid talking about them.
One conversation can last for years in my head - as one day in the shower, I think of the perfect retort to something someone said in 1998.
Sam didn't report to me, but was a key part of my team's main deliverable. I had responsibility for the outcome - but limited authority over his work.
Instead of accusing Sam, I'd enlist him to help figure out a way to avoid it happening again.

Instead of treating this as a Sam problem, I framed it as a breakdown in the process. My ultimate goal wasn't to assign blame - it was to make sure the executive team had what they needed going forward.
Framing a situation as a shared problem rather than an accusation makes conversations more productive, sometimes surfaces deeper issues, and helps preserve working relationships.
It does NOT work when someone is causing harm to others or to the organization. Bullying, harassment, ethical lapses - those aren't process issues, they're boundary violations.
